status: One additive, source-checked Canadian knowledge claim and original untested teaching design. No existing claim, interval or dependency is changed; no learner attainment or publication is inferred.

newCard.subject: Personal & Social Development
newCard.name: Rights and civic responsibilities in Canada
newCard.description: Know selected rights and freedoms in Canada—equal protection under law, freedom of religion and expression, and eligible citizens’ federal voting rights—and explain related responsibilities to respect others’ rights, obey laws and contribute to community life. Distinguish general protections from citizenship/age-qualified voting, and legal duties from voluntary civic contributions.
evidence: After study, explain equal protection under law and freedom of religion and expression in simple Canadian public-life cases. Recognise that general protections are not reserved only for citizens or Canadian-born people, and that rights are not unlimited permission to harm others.

Distinguish general protections from the basic federal elector qualifications of Canadian citizenship and being at least 18 on polling day. Recognise that actual voting also has procedures, and that a primary-age child can have rights and participate in community life without being qualified to cast a federal vote.

Explain responsibilities to obey laws and respect others’ rights, and describe a voluntary way to contribute to civic/community life. Do not make rights conditional on volunteering or agreeing with a political opinion; distinguish a government-related Charter question from every private disagreement.
newCard.assessmentPrompt: A newcomer, a child and an adult citizen discuss a public decision in Canada. Can {{name}} explain their protections for equal treatment under law, religion and expression, who has the basic qualifications for a federal vote, and how they can act responsibly? Would someone have to volunteer to keep those rights?

pedagogy.summary: Teach a bounded Canadian public-life rights/eligibility/responsibility repertoire through factual contrasts, not generic kindness or memorised political slogans.
bestPractices: Keep general protections and citizen/age-qualified federal voting visibly separate.
Require explanations on new fictional cases, not only sorting labels.
Separate government Charter application, other private rules/laws, legal duties and voluntary civic contributions.
keyRepresentations: Fictional persons with explicitly supplied relevant qualification facts
Changed-case cards that vary one relevant fact
commonMisconceptions: Only citizens or Canadian-born people have freedom of religion or expression.
Every citizen, including a child, may cast a federal vote.
Rights must be earned by volunteering or agreeing with the government.
A civic responsibility to vote means federal voting is legally compulsory.
Every private disagreement is directly a Charter case.

learn.summary: Learn the selected Canadian protections and qualification distinctions, then explain responsible choices and transfer without private disclosure.

activities.title: Rights, qualification and responsibility in supplied Canadian cases
learnerActions: Adult setup: Prepare original short, attributed rights/eligibility/responsibility summaries from the selected official passages. Explain that the Charter constrains government and that other rules/laws can still matter in private relationships; do not turn this into a legal test of a real dispute. Teach the named protections in ordinary language without requiring section numbers, exact constitutional wording or a complete rights catalogue.

Use supplied fictional cases involving a government/public decision: a newcomer’s religious practice or opinion and equal treatment under law. Ask what protection is relevant and why citizenship, name, accent or birthplace alone does not remove those general protections. Do not ask for the learner’s or family’s religion, immigration/citizenship status or personal legal history.

Compare fictional people whose relevant facts are explicitly supplied: a 30-year-old Canadian citizen, a 30-year-old newcomer who is not a citizen, and a 10-year-old Canadian citizen. Identify who has the basic federal elector qualifications and who still has general protections. Explain that citizenship and age are not inferred from appearance and that qualification is distinct from completing the actual registration/identification procedures. No voting simulation or administrative document is required for this knowledge claim.

Sort and explain a small set of responsibilities/contributions: obeying laws, respecting another person’s protected freedoms, becoming informed, voting when qualified, and choosing a suitable community-helping activity. Explain that civic responsibility to vote is not compulsory federal voting, and a chosen volunteer action is not a price paid to earn rights. Do not equate inability to volunteer, adult employment or agreement with a viewpoint with a person’s worth or rights.

Remove the completed explanatory key. Ask the learner to explain all three named protections, the qualified voting distinction and a supported responsibility/contribution response in their own words. A right-name match without the distinction or rationale is only a partial check. Adult reading of a case can remove incidental literacy load; the learner supplies the knowledge/explanation.

Change one relevant fact at a time: a person becomes 18 on polling day, a newcomer becomes a Canadian citizen, or a disagreement is between private friends rather than a government decision. Ask what changes and what does not. Where the scenario is insufficient, ask what fact or official guidance would be needed; no real legal entitlement or private case is adjudicated.

Use a new fictional public-life/community scenario to check transfer of the same Canadian repertoire. Keep generic kind behaviour and campaign planning separate: they support participation but cannot substitute for the actual rights/eligibility knowledge. No real political message, petition, enrolment, personal disclosure, learner-state change or party preference is required.
activities.intendedInsight: People can share general protections while differing in voting qualification; rights and responsible participation do not depend on status stereotypes or earning approval.
feedback: Ask which protection or qualification fact supports the answer.
Separate the right from a person’s citizenship/age and from whether an action is a legal duty or a voluntary contribution.
If the case concerns a private disagreement or missing facts, identify that limit rather than inventing a court outcome.
activities.rationale: Original untested teaching design; factual verification does not establish teaching efficacy.
sourceClaims: The public guide distinguishes general protections on arrival from citizenship-specific voting and describes law/respect/community responsibilities.
General protections, citizen-specific exceptions, reasonable limits and the Charter’s application to governments are distinct.
The basic elector qualifications are Canadian citizenship and age 18 or older on polling day. The short section itself was read; no whole-Act review is claimed.
Federal voting is voluntary. Only this selected fact is relied on here, not its unrelated division-of-powers summary or a changing riding count.
Obeying laws, respecting public obligations and helping community/environment are distinguished from a personal choice of volunteer activity.

constraints: Fixed learned repertoire is the selected Canadian equal-protection/religion/expression, basic federal elector qualification and responsibilities distinction. New scenarios support transfer; a different country’s rules do not silently replace these facts.

The Charter applies to government; the child is not required to adjudicate section 1 limits, litigation, private human-rights-code cases or constitutional division of powers. Other laws may protect people in private settings.

Federal qualification is not every election’s full procedure. Do not generalise this rule to every municipal, school-board or Indigenous election, require identity documents or teach current electoral schedules/riding counts.

No requirement for full jury-service, military, adult employment, constitutional-history, parliamentary-procedure, party or rights-section inventories. Basic relevant vocabulary supports explanation without a new hard gate to every generic ethics term.
No real-life personal status/religion/legal disclosure, moral-worth ranking, actual external political action or inference of learner mastery. Original teaching efficacy remains untested.
reviewNotes: 2026-11-11: original bounded knowledge curation after whole-card comparison with community rights, ethics vocabulary, rules/laws, civic action, Australian democracy/history and Ontario local-governance claims. Official factual passages checked as specified; no classroom intervention result or general learner transfer inferred.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A newcomer, a child and an adult citizen discuss a public decision in Canada. Can {{name}} explain their protections for equal treatment under law, religion and expression, who has the basic qualifications for a federal vote, and how they can act responsibly? Would someone have to volunteer to keep those rights?
assess.correctAnswer: Explains the named general protections, correctly distinguishes basic federal voter qualification and government/private scope, and gives a justified responsibility/contribution response without rights-as-reward or compulsory-vote inference.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Newcomer/child/adult contrasts distinguish actual rights and qualification knowledge from generic kindness or treating all rights as citizen-only. Changing one relevant fact tests which rule explains the decision, while a private-case near miss exposes an overgeneralised Charter claim.
probeDeeper: Which named protection applies, and is citizenship needed for it?
Which supplied age/citizenship fact changes basic federal voter qualification?
Is this a legal duty, a civic responsibility or a chosen way to help—and does declining to volunteer remove a right?
Does this concern a government decision or a private disagreement? What can we say without inventing a legal judgment?

errorPatterns.pattern: Restricts all general protections to citizens or extends all voting qualifications to children.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Removes a newcomer’s religious freedom or gives a 10-year-old a federal vote simply because they are a citizen.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild the general-protections versus qualified-voting distinction using explicitly supplied facts.

errorPatterns.pattern: Makes rights conditional on volunteering, agreement or compulsory participation.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says a person loses rights for not volunteering, or that civic voting responsibility means a legal requirement to cast a federal vote.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate legal obligations and protections from the particular chosen civic contribution.

errorPatterns.pattern: Applies a government Charter rule to every private disagreement.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats an argument between fictional friends as automatically a direct Charter violation.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Identify the public/government context and acknowledge that other rules/laws can matter without deciding a real case.

responseLevels.gap: Only generic respect/kindness labels, with no actual Canadian protections or qualification distinction.
responseLevels.partial: Names some protections but confuses citizenship/age, rights-as-reward, government scope or responsibilities.
responseLevels.full: Explains the complete bounded repertoire on changed supplied cases, retaining general-versus-qualified and duty-versus-contribution distinctions without overclaiming a legal decision.

actions: Teach and assess the complete bounded card and original guide, including actual named general protections, basic qualified federal voting and civic responsibilities. The original supplied cases test the distinctions without private status disclosure.

Require a responsibility that respects others’ rights and a suitable way to contribute to public/community life. Distinguish law, civic responsibility and chosen volunteer action rather than treating all obligations as either compulsory or optional.

Use a changed government/public-life case and explain which rule applies, what citizenship/age information matters and what remains outside the basic scope. Preserve the limits on private Charter disputes and on federal versus every possible electoral procedure.

limits: The repertoire concerns particular Canadian public-life knowledge; existing community respect, ethics vocabulary and Australian election/history claims retain their full separate meanings.
Official factual verification is not a teaching intervention study. No generic vocabulary hard gate, automatic skill transfer or learner estimate reset is introduced.
This one record does not complete Grade5 or Ontario. Other mandatory source records require their own whole-claim/task review.
